reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India national programmes
clinicalPearls: Caused by the spore-forming Gram-positive rod Bacillus anthracis, a zoonosis of herbivores acquired through contact with infected animals or contaminated animal products
Cutaneous anthrax is the commonest form and presents as a painless papule that ulcerates into a characteristic black eschar with marked surrounding oedema
Inhalational (pulmonary) anthrax follows spore inhalation and causes a fulminant illness with a widened mediastinum from haemorrhagic lymphadenitis and rapidly fatal shock
Gastrointestinal and oropharyngeal forms follow ingestion of contaminated meat and carry high mortality
It is a recognised agent of bioterrorism, so clustered or unexplained inhalational cases warrant urgent public-health alert
Prompt antibacterial therapy is effective for cutaneous disease, while systemic forms also require antitoxin and intensive supportive care
In endemic parts of India it occurs sporadically among people handling livestock, hides and wool
Diagnosis rests on Gram stain and culture of lesion, blood or other fluids, with PCR and toxin assays as confirmatory tests
reference.pathophysiology: Bacillus anthracis spores enter through skin abrasions, inhalation or ingestion, germinate, and multiply while producing a poly-D-glutamic acid capsule that resists phagocytosis and a tripartite toxin. Protective antigen mediates entry of lethal factor and oedema factor into cells; lethal factor is a protease that disrupts intracellular signalling and triggers massive inflammatory and cytotoxic effects, while oedema factor raises cyclic AMP causing the striking tissue oedema. Systemic dissemination produces toxaemia, vascular leak, haemorrhage and shock, which drive the high mortality of non-cutaneous disease.
additionalDifferentials: Staphylococcal or streptococcal skin and soft-tissue infection with eschar
Community-acquired pneumonia or mediastinitis for the inhalational form
infectionMimics: Brown recluse spider bite with necrotic eschar
Orf or other zoonotic skin lesions
additionalInvestigations: Gram stain and culture of skin lesion fluid, blood, pleural fluid or CSF
Chest imaging looking for a widened mediastinum and pleural effusions in inhalational anthrax
PCR and toxin/antigen detection for rapid confirmation
Notification to and testing by a reference/public-health laboratory
redFlags: Widened mediastinum with dyspnoea and shock indicating inhalational anthrax, a medical emergency
Extensive oedema of the head and neck threatening the airway in cutaneous or oropharyngeal disease
Signs of meningitis (anthrax meningoencephalitis is often haemorrhagic and rapidly fatal)
A cluster of unexplained severe febrile respiratory illnesses suggesting deliberate release
reference.prognosis: Cutaneous anthrax usually responds well to timely antibacterial treatment with low mortality, though the eschar heals with scarring. Inhalational, gastrointestinal and meningeal forms are frequently fatal even with treatment, and outcome depends critically on how early therapy and antitoxin are started.
pitfalls: Incising or debriding a cutaneous anthrax lesion, which can worsen dissemination
Mistaking early inhalational anthrax for ordinary influenza or community-acquired pneumonia and delaying therapy
Failing to consider occupational or bioterrorism exposure history
Overlooking the need for antitoxin and public-health notification in systemic disease
management: Prompt antibacterial therapy with a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin or with doxycycline, using combination intravenous regimens that include a protein-synthesis inhibitor for systemic disease
Add antitoxin therapy — a monoclonal anti-protective-antigen agent or anthrax immune globulin — for inhalational, gastrointestinal or meningeal forms
Intensive supportive care for toxaemic shock and vascular leak, with fluid resuscitation, vasopressors and organ support
Drainage of pleural effusions and other haemorrhagic collections to remove toxin and relieve compromise
Extend the antibacterial course with central nervous system-penetrating agents where meningitis is present
Urgent notification to public-health authorities and reference-laboratory confirmation, with post-exposure antibacterial prophylaxis and vaccination for exposed contacts

valueTables.title: CDC category A, B and C bioterrorism agents

cells.text: Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis); botulism (Clostridium botulinum toxin); plague (Yersinia pestis); smallpox (Variola major); tularemia (Francisella tularensis); viral hemorrhagic fevers: arenaviruses (Lassa, New World: Machupo, Junin, Guanarito and Sabia), Bunyaviridae (Crimean-Congo, Rift Valley), Filoviridae (Ebola, Marburg)

Brucellosis (Brucella spp.); epsilon toxin of Clostridium perfringens; food safety threats (for example Salmonella spp., Escherichia coli O157:H7, Shigella); glanders (Burkholderia mallei); melioidosis (B. pseudomallei); psittacosis (Chlamydophila psittaci); Q fever (Coxiella burnetii); ricin toxin from Ricinus communis (castor beans); staphylococcal enterotoxin B; typhus fever (Rickettsia prowazekii); viral encephalitis [alphaviruses, for example Venezuelan, eastern and western equine encephalitis]; water safety threats (for example Vibrio cholerae, Cryptosporidium parvum)
Emerging infectious disease threats such as Nipah, hantavirus, SARS coronavirus and pandemic influenza
